Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the failing test does
  - It creates a SummaryStatistics, overrides the mean implementation with a new Mean(), adds values 1, 2, 3, 4, and then asserts that stats.getMean() equals (new Mean()).evaluate(scores).
- How SummaryStatistics currently computes aggregates
  - addValue(double) always updates internal moments and basic stats (sumImpl, sumsqImpl, minImpl, maxImpl, sumLogImpl, and secondMoment).
  - Crucially, it only forwards increments to the override implementations if they are not the library defaults:
    - If meanImpl is not an instance of Mean, it calls meanImpl.increment(value).
    - If varianceImpl is not an instance of Variance, it calls varianceImpl.increment(value).
    - If geoMeanImpl is not an instance of GeometricMean, it calls geoMeanImpl.increment(value).
  - getMean() simply returns meanImpl.getResult().
  - getVariance() returns varianceImpl.getResult().
  - getStandardDeviation() returns sqrt(getVariance()) when n > 1, 0 when n == 1, and NaN when n == 0.

- Why the test fails
  - The test calls stats.setMeanImpl(new Mean()) before adding values. This passes the emptiness check (checkEmpty()) and assigns meanImpl to a plain Mean instance.
  - In addValue, because meanImpl is an instance of Mean, the code does not call meanImpl.increment(value) (lines 156–163).
  - The default design assumes that if meanImpl is a Mean, it will be internally wired to the shared secondMoment so it can compute the mean without receiving explicit increments. However, setMeanImpl does not wire the provided Mean to the internal secondMoment; it just assigns the reference (lines 605–608).
  - As a result, the overridden Mean receives neither increments nor a reference to secondMoment, so meanImpl.getResult() remains NaN. Therefore, stats.getMean() returns NaN, and the assertion against the correct mean fails.

- Relation to the reported bug (setVarianceImpl causes NaN standard deviation)
  - The same pattern exists for variance: setVarianceImpl just assigns the provided statistic (lines 634–637) and addValue does not increment varianceImpl when it is an instance of Variance (lines 161–163).
  - If a user calls setVarianceImpl(new Variance(false)) or new Variance(true), the new Variance instance is neither incremented nor wired to secondMoment. Consequently, varianceImpl.getResult() stays NaN, and getStandardDeviation() computes sqrt(NaN) which yields NaN for n > 1.
  - This exactly matches the reported issue: overriding variance implementation leads to NaN standard deviation.

- Root cause
  - The setter methods setMeanImpl and setVarianceImpl fail to integrate the provided built-in implementations (Mean, Variance) with the internal state (secondMoment) that SummaryStatistics maintains and relies upon when it chooses not to increment those implementations directly in addValue.
  - The logic in addValue that skips incrementing when meanImpl is a Mean (or varianceImpl is a Variance) only works if those instances are properly wired to the shared secondMoment. Because the setters don’t perform this wiring, overriding with Mean/Variance breaks the computations and results in NaN.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
